transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 min
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Lena Morales (Redwood CSM); Daniel Park (Kodama Head of ML), Sophia Liao (Eng Manager), Marco Suarez (CTO), Aisha Khan (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Goal: Understand cost per token levers and hosting path (hosted -> dedicated -> private) for Kodama's real-time ML assistant product.
- Kodama target: 50k daily tokens initially, budget ~6k/mo but can expand if ROI clear.
- Key asks: clarity on per-token math, batching/caching tradeoffs, SLA for p95 latency, security (SOC2, SSO, KMS).

Topics: Cost/unit economics, batch/cache levers, hosting tradeoffs, pilot scope, security needs

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do intros quick then jump into what you're trying to solve. I'm Alex, AE here at Redwood, and Priya on the line is our SE who lives in inference land.
[00:18] Daniel Park: Hi Alex, thanks. I'm Daniel, head of ML at Kodama. We build a real-time assistant for enterprise clients, hoping to reduce inference spend but keep p95 under 300 ms for short prompts.
[00:29] Sophia Liao: Sophia here, engineering manager. We're seeing big ops spikes and want to understand the hosted vs dedicated cost math.
[00:36] Priya Rao: Thanks — quick clarifying q, are you mostly concerned about per-token bill, or do you have throughput/latency constraints first?
[00:46] Marco Suarez: Both. We have a budget line for model infra, roughly $6k a month at pilot, but it's soft. Main thing is user experience latency <350 ms p95 for short interactions.
[00:56] Alex Chen: Great, that frames it. Quick note on our side: hosted gives fastest start, dedicated reserved capacity lowers unit cost with commit, private is for strict residency/air-gapped needs and higher ops. We'll run through a per-token breakdown and batching/caching knobs.
[01:12] Aisha Khan: Also need to confirm we can meet our customer's data residency; some clients want EU-only.
[01:19] Priya Rao: Noted. On-EU regions for hosted are possible; private deployment supports full control.

[03:05] Alex Chen: Ok digging into numbers. You mentioned 50k daily tokens — is that inference tokens, or includes embeddings and other jobs?
[03:12] Daniel Park: That's generation tokens from active users only. Embeddings are separate but relatively small right now.
[03:20] Priya Rao: For a 50k/day gen baseline, we usually model per-token cost with three levers: raw compute price (hosted per-token), batching efficiency, and cache hit rate. Also model size/quantization matters.
[03:35] Alex Chen: Quick example: hosted for a mid-size decoder model family might be $0.0009 per token at baseline with small batching, but with better batching and prefix/KV cache hits that realized cost can fall to $0.00045/token. If you do a dedicated reserved pool, committed pricing can push units lower — maybe $0.00025/token depending on commit and workload shape. Those numbers are illustrative.
[04:03] Marco Suarez: Can you explain prefix/KV cache again? We've heard of it but not sure of the ops implications.
[04:09] Priya Rao: Sure — prefix or KV cache stores repeated context so repeated tokens don't re-run the whole compute path. For example, if users often reuse the same system prompt or chunk of conversation, cache hits reduce compute. The tradeoff is cache memory footprint and warmup costs.
[04:25] Sophia Liao: So cache hit rate is workload dependent. Any roughs for e.g., a customer service assistant?
[04:32] Priya Rao: For structured assistants we've seen 20–40% effective token reduction from prefix caching across sessions; if you do conversation-level caching it can be higher. But depends on prompt engineering.

[06:00] Daniel Park: Your hosted pricing is per token — do you meter input+output? How do you count?
[06:08] Alex Chen: We meter per-token for generation (input tokens + output tokens typically counted), though we'll show the exact formula in the pricing sheet we'll send. Dedicated often lets you move to flat compute reservations where unit math is about GPU utilization and throughput.
[06:23] Aisha Khan: If we're capacity planning, what throughput can a single dedicated pool handle? We have spiky traffic.
[06:30] Priya Rao: Depends on model and batch size; e.g., a 70B quantized model on a V100-ish equivalent (we'll be more specific in the performance note) can handle X tokens/s with batching, but p95 increases with batch window. We can simulate expected p95 vs batch window.

[08:15] Alex Chen: Important trade: aggressive batching improves tokens per GPU but hurts tail latency. So if your p95 target is strict, we might recommend a hybrid route — smaller batch window for latency-critical routes, and larger for background summarization.
[08:31] Marco Suarez: Does Redwood support multi-route policies? Like route critical calls to low-latency pool and async to cheaper pool?
[08:38] Priya Rao: Yes — routing policies allow per-route SLOs and fallback to cheaper model variants when capacity tight.

[10:02] Sophia Liao: We also worry about cold starts and KV cache warmup after deploy — what's typical impact on early requests?
[10:09] Priya Rao: Cold starts can show higher latency until KV caches warm. We recommend warmup probes during rollout and can keep a small warmed pool. That does cost a bit but reduces p95 spikes.

[12:44] Daniel Park: Back to cost math — how do quantization steps change numbers? We're using a 33B family today.
[12:52] Priya Rao: Quantization reduces memory and can increase batch size; many customers see 20–40% lower unit compute cost moving 33B to 4-bit or 8-bit quantized runtimes, albeit with some accuracy tradeoffs you should validate. We'll propose model-specific quant profiles in the follow-up.

[15:00] Alex Chen: Let's build a sample scenario: 50k/day, average prompt+response 40 tokens per request, that's ~2M tokens/month. At hosted $0.0009/token that's $1,800/mo baseline; with caching and batching maybe $900/mo. If dedicated reserved and good utilization maybe $500/mo equivalent. These are back-of-envelope.
[15:28] Marco Suarez: Wait that math's lower than our $6k budget — are we missing something?
[15:34] Alex Chen: The budget includes overhead — monitoring, retention of logs, standby capacity for spikes, and often enterprises plan for throughput peaks. Also embeddings and additional pipelines can add cost. The $6k might map to a future scale or include safety margins.

[17:10] Sophia Liao: What's the min commitment for dedicated?
[17:15] Alex Chen: Typically monthly reserved capacity tiers start at several thousand dollars per month — depends on GPU types and commit length. We can model a 3-month pilot with lower commit and option to convert to annual for better unit math.

[19:30] Aisha Khan: On security — we need SOC2, SSO (SAML/Okta), audit logs, and KMS integration. Also EU data residency. Can you confirm hosted covers these?
[19:40] Priya Rao: Hosted supports SOC2, SAML SSO integrations and KMS for key wrapping. We maintain audit logs; we'll share the security pack. For EU residency, we host in eu-west region; for strict residency or air-gapped customers, Private is the choice.
[20:02] Daniel Park: Good. Any additional compliance add-ons cost?
[20:07] Alex Chen: Some enterprise compliance add-ons (longer log retention, dedicated logging, custom KMS/HSM integrations) are extras — we'll call those out in the security pack.

[22:45] Marco Suarez: Mechanically, how does dedicated differ for networking? Do we need VPC peering or can we use private link?
[22:54] Priya Rao: Either. Dedicated typically supports VPC peering or PrivateLink, depending on cloud. For Private deployment we provide a private control plane and customer-managed networking. We'll need your network team to review the diagram.

[25:10] Alex Chen: Let's talk risk: if you go hosted and later need to move to private, we support model versioning and migration plans. The biggest friction is KV formats and your data flows; we help export and rehydrate caches where possible.

[27:00] Sophia Liao: For pilot scope, we want a small hosted test with SSO and EU region for select clients, and a dedicated cost model to compare. Could you run a cost compare for 3 scenarios: hosted pilot only, hosted->dedicated at 6 months, and private if residency enforced?
[27:15] Alex Chen: Yes we'll build that. We'll include token math and also the ops/time costs for your team to manage private.

[29:40] Priya Rao: Quick note on measurements — to compare apples-to-apples we'll need your request traces (token distribution, seq length distribution, concurrency) and typical session reuse rates. Even a sampled day helps.
[29:52] Daniel Park: We can share anonymized traces. Aisha can upload.
[30:00] Aisha Khan: I'll generate a sanitized sample by 2027-07-14. 

[32:20] Marco Suarez: One objection — we've used OpenCloudAI and their unit pricing seemed simpler; why Redwood?
[32:28] Alex Chen: Fair. Redwood focuses on production predictability — routing policies, explicit batch/cache levers, and tooling to reduce unit economics. We provide transparent SLOs and a migration path across hosting types.

[34:10] Daniel Park: Are there any hard minimums for response latency on dedicated? We need p95 under 350ms.
[34:18] Priya Rao: We'll run a simulated profile. With smaller batch windows and GPU selection tuned to your model we believe it's achievable. We'll quantify in the perf note.

[36:45] Sophia Liao: On instrumentation, does Redwood provide token-level cost breakdown in the console?
[36:50] Alex Chen: Yes — the console gives token-level and route-level breakdowns, traces, and cost per token per-model dashboards. You can set alerts on cost deltas and quality regression too.

[39:00] Priya Rao: Another nuance: when you have spiky loads, autoscaling and burst capacity are relevant. Dedicated allows burst into extra capacity in some tiers; hosted can also burst. But burst pricing has different economics.

[41:30] Marco Suarez: If we commit annually, can we get reserved GPU-type guarantees?
[41:36] Alex Chen: Yes, with dedicated annual contracts we can reserve particular instance classes and guarantee min throughput for your pool.

[43:50] Daniel Park: What's the typical onboarding timeline for a hosted pilot with SSO and EU region?
[43:56] Lena Morales: For a basic hosted pilot with SSO and region selection, we usually do 2–3 weeks (account, keys, SSO, sample models). If you need dedicated network setup or private deploy, add 3–6 weeks.

[46:12] Aisha Khan: Any sample artifacts or spreadsheets we can use to plug our numbers?
[46:17] Alex Chen: Yes — we'll send a pricing workbook and pilot template (link: https://redwood.example.com/pricing/pilot-workbook) and the security pack (https://redwood.example.com/security-pack).

[48:40] Priya Rao: A few quick technical caveats — quant profiles are model-specific; some open models tolerate 4-bit quant better than others. Also multi-tenant hosted environments limit some aggressive tuning we do in dedicated.

[51:00] Sophia Liao: If we do a pilot, can we run a short bench to measure p95 at our token distribution?
[51:07] Priya Rao: Absolutely. We can run a 48-hour bench on hosted with your traces and provide p50/p95 and cost per token report. We'll need the sanitized traces.

[53:25] Marco Suarez: What's the escalation path if SLA breaks?
[53:30] Lena Morales: For committed dedicated customers we have SLA and an escalation matrix; for hosted we have support tiers with SLAs in enterprise plans. We'll send the SLA doc.

[55:10] Daniel Park: OK good recap — Daniel: want hosted pilot in EU, SSO, bench using our traces — see cost scenarios for hosted vs dedicated vs private; Redwood to send pricing workbook and security docs.
[55:24] Alex Chen: Yup. Recap for Redwood: 1) send pricing workbook and three cost slices; 2) security pack and network diagram; 3) perform bench plan for 48-hour pilot on hosted with sanitized traces; 4) schedule scoping session week of 7/19.
[55:40] Sophia Liao: Sounds good.
[55:45] Aisha Khan: I'll upload traces and network constraints by 7/14.
[55:49] Alex Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the artifacts and calendar invite.
[56:02] Marco Suarez: Thanks.
[56:05] Daniel Park: Appreciate it.

End of call.
